title: Read key = value settings from a config file in a bash script
summary: Reads a plain settings file, skips comments and blank lines, and gives you either all settings or the value of one key. Spaces around the equals sign are allowed.

steps.explain: Save the script. Create the file with nano and paste the whole text, including the first line that starts with #!. Press Ctrl+O then Enter to save, and Ctrl+X to exit.
steps.expect: An empty editor opens. After you save, the file exists in the current folder.

steps.explain: Check the script for syntax mistakes without running it.
steps.expect: No output means the syntax is correct.

steps.explain: Make the script executable so you can start it by its name.
steps.expect: No output. ls -l then shows x in the permissions.

steps.explain: Create a settings file with a comment, a blank line, a broken line and a few settings.
steps.cmd:
printf '# app settings
backup_dir = /home/user/backups
keep_days=14
  name =  my laptop  
url=http://example.com/?a=b

broken line
' > app.conf
steps.expect: No output. The file app.conf now exists.

steps.explain: Print all settings in alphabetical order. The broken line gives a warning on STDERR and is skipped.
steps.expect: warning: line 7 has no '=', skipped: broken line, then backup_dir = /home/user/backups, keep_days = 14, name = my laptop, url = http://example.com/?a=b

steps.explain: Print the value of one key only.
Ask for a key that does not exist. The script prints an error and exits with code 1.
steps.expect: error: key 'nope' not found in app.conf, then exit code 1

warnings: The script reads only KEY = VALUE lines. Never load a config file with the . or source command in a script: it runs any shell code inside the file.
Everything after the first equals sign is the value, including any # text. A comment at the end of a line becomes part of the value.
Values are plain text. Quotes around a value are kept as part of it.

script.content:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# read-config.sh - read key = value settings from a config file.
# Usage: ./read-config.sh CONFIG_FILE [KEY]
# Each setting is one line: key = value (spaces around = are optional).
# Lines that start with # and empty lines are ignored.
# Without KEY, every setting is printed. With KEY, only that value is printed.

set -euo pipefail

if (( $# < 1 || $# > 2 )) || [[ ! -r "$1" ]]; then
    echo "usage: $0 CONFIG_FILE [KEY]" >&2
    exit 2
fi
CONFIG=$1
WANTED=${2:-}

declare -A settings=()
line_no=0

# IFS= keeps leading spaces; -r stops backslashes from being treated specially.
# "|| [[ -n $line ]]" also handles a last line that has no newline at its end.
while IFS= read -r line || [[ -n $line ]]; do
    line_no=$((line_no + 1))

    # Remove spaces and tabs at the start and at the end of the line.
    line=${line#"${line%%[![:space:]]*}"}
    line=${line%"${line##*[![:space:]]}"}

    # Skip empty lines and comments.
    if [[ -z $line || $line == \#* ]]; then
        continue
    fi
    if [[ $line != *=* ]]; then
        echo "warning: line $line_no has no '=', skipped: $line" >&2
        continue
    fi

    # Split at the FIRST '=': the key is before it, the value is after it.
    key=${line%%=*}
    value=${line#*=}
    key=${key%"${key##*[![:space:]]}"}      # trim spaces after the key
    value=${value#"${value%%[![:space:]]*}"} # trim spaces before the value
    settings[$key]=$value
done < "$CONFIG"

if [[ -n $WANTED ]]; then
    if [[ -z ${settings[$WANTED]+set} ]]; then
        echo "error: key '$WANTED' not found in $CONFIG" >&2
        exit 1
    fi
    echo "${settings[$WANTED]}"
else
    # Print every key in sorted order.
    while IFS= read -r key; do
        echo "$key = ${settings[$key]}"
    done < <(printf '%s\n' "${!settings[@]}" | sort)
fi

prerequisites: A Linux terminal with bash 4 or newer
